candidates.name: python-mwviews
candidates.what_it_holds: Python client library (MIT, ~38 commits, 67 stars) for the Wikimedia pageviews API and static pageview dumps. Query per-article views, per-project views, and top-N articles by project/access-method/agent-type at daily/monthly granularity back to July 2015 (API) with dump-parsing support for older static counts. No data committed; pure acquisition tooling.
candidates.why_useful: Directly builds Gap 5 (Wikipedia pageviews tooling as an engagement/destination-demand proxy) — a maintained, well-documented one-command way to pull pageviews for any city/attraction/landmark Wikipedia article (e.g. 'New York City', 'Eiffel Tower', destination pages) as a free, high-frequency, near-real-time travel-interest signal comparable to Google Trends but with committable raw counts instead of blocked normalization.
candidates.time_coverage: API: July 2015-present daily; static dumps back further with separate parsing
candidates.last_activity: unspecified exact date; actively maintained per repo stats

candidates.name: wikipediatrend
candidates.what_it_holds: R package (GPL>=2, v2.1.6 released 2020-06-03) with wp_trend() to retrieve per-article Wikipedia pageview time series by language/article, returning a tidy date/lang/article/views data frame. Critically, it stitches together historical pre-2016 data (pre-dating the official API, sourced from a Hertie School of Governance-commissioned archive hosted at petermeissner.de) with the post-2016 official Wikimedia Foundation API, giving continuous coverage back to as early as 2007-2008 for some articles.
candidates.why_useful: Fills the point-in-time/history-depth problem directly: our stated gap is that Google Trends pulls are not point-in-time and pageviews tooling generally starts in 2015. This gives longer (2007+) continuous history for city/destination/attraction Wikipedia articles as a demand proxy usable for longer backtests than the official API alone allows.

candidates.name: statsgrokse
candidates.what_it_holds: R binding (GPL>=2, last release 2017-03-22) to the now-defunct stats.grok.se pageview mirror, covering Wikipedia pageview counts 2008-2015 (the pre-official-API era) by article/language/date range.
candidates.why_useful: Companion/underlying tool to wikipediatrend's historical stitch; useful if that package's hosted historical mirror ever goes down, since it hits the original stats.grok.se archive directly for 2008-2015 city/destination article views.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Same historical window as part of wikipediatrend's pipeline

candidates.name: wiki-download-parse-page-views
candidates.what_it_holds: Python pipeline (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences) that downloads, filters and aggregates Wikipedia's original hourly/monthly static pagecount dumps from before the 2015 API existed, for a user-specified list of pages and year range, outputting aggregated annual CSV view counts per page. 12 commits; no license file found; notes the dump server throttles to 3 concurrent threads.
candidates.why_useful: A second, independent route (besides wikipediatrend/statsgrokse) to reconstruct pre-2015 pageview history for any set of destination/city Wikipedia articles directly from Wikimedia's own raw dump archive rather than a third-party mirror — reduces single-point-of-failure risk for the historical-depth use case in Gap 4/5.
candidates.time_coverage: pre-2015 (exact start depends on Wikimedia dump availability, commonly from Dec 2007)
candidates.size_hint: pipeline only, no committed data (downloads from dumps.wikimedia.org at runtime)

candidates.name: waxer
candidates.what_it_holds: Official Wikimedia R package wrapping the Analytics Query Service (AQS) /metrics REST endpoint (pageviews, unique devices, edits, registered users) for any Wikimedia project. MIT licensed, 24 commits, actively maintained by the Wikimedia Foundation itself.
candidates.why_useful: First-party, presumably most-stable client for the same pageviews API as python-mwviews/pageviews.js, useful if the team's forecasting stack is R-based (the ADR/margin work already uses R-adjacent tooling in places) for pulling destination-article pageviews as an engagement proxy.
candidates.last_activity: unspecified, actively maintained per Wikimedia org
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: same API as python-mwviews / pageviews.js, different language binding

candidates.name: pageviews.js
candidates.what_it_holds: Lightweight JavaScript/Node client (Apache-2.0, Thomas Steiner, 2017, 63 commits) for the Wikimedia Pageviews API: per-article views, project totals, top articles, unique-device counts by time granularity.
candidates.why_useful: A JS alternative to python-mwviews/waxer for the same pageviews-as-engagement-proxy use case; only worth using if the team ever needs a browser/Node-side pull (e.g. a lightweight dashboard) rather than a Python/R backtest pipeline.

candidates.name: pageviews (Pageviews Analysis)
candidates.what_it_holds: Full-stack (PHP/JS) web application, the WMF-hosted 'Pageviews Analysis' tool at pageviews.wmcloud.org, for interactively comparing pageview trends across articles/projects. MIT licensed, 1,426 commits, 164 stars/43 forks. Archived Sept 2026 and migrated to GitLab, but the underlying API it hits (Wikimedia AQS) is unaffected.
candidates.why_useful: Not directly a data source for our pipeline (it is a browser UI, not an API client library to embed), but is the reference implementation showing exactly what pageview granularities/filters (agent type, access method, per-project) are available - useful for spec'ing a pull. Low direct utility since the repo itself is archived and UI-only.

candidates.name: kaggle-web-traffic (1st place solution, Wikipedia Web Traffic Forecasting)
candidates.what_it_holds: 1st-place solution code (MIT license) for Google/Kaggle's 'Web Traffic Time Series Forecasting' competition, which itself is built on a public dataset of ~145,000 Wikipedia articles' daily pageviews (train_2.csv/key_2.csv, roughly Jul 2015-Sep 2017, multiple languages including many city/country/landmark/tourism-related articles). Data must be pulled from Kaggle (kaggle.com/c/web-traffic-time-series-forecasting) rather than the repo itself; repo only has the RNN encoder-decoder modeling code.
candidates.why_useful: The underlying Kaggle dataset (pointer, not in this repo) is a large, ready-made multi-year daily pageview panel across ~145k Wikipedia articles in several languages, which almost certainly includes major tourist-destination cities/landmarks/countries as dense daily series 2015-2017 - useful as a historical validation set for 'does city pageview level/growth lead STR/hotel demand' even though it predates the Airbnb-relevant recent quarters. Also a source of mixed-frequency/time-series forecasting method ideas (Gap 17).
candidates.geography: global, multi-language Wikipedia (city/country/landmark articles included among the ~145k)
candidates.size_hint: 145,000 time series x ~800 days; dataset lives on Kaggle, repo is code-only
candidates.license: MIT (code); Kaggle competition data terms apply to the dataset itself

candidates.name: attention-flow
candidates.what_it_holds: Active research repo (MIT, 73 commits, daily CI) using daily Wikipedia pageviews as a free 'market attention' proxy for ~34 entities/39 edges across four 2020-2026 economic-narrative graphs (AI buildout, GLP-1, EV/battery, COVID). Caches raw pageview pulls under data/raw/, trains a GRU+graph-attention network to forecast one-week-ahead 'attention shocks', and publishes live graded forecast-accuracy JSON (data.json, track.json) via a running demo.
candidates.why_useful: Not itself a tourism dataset, but a live, working, actively-updated methodological template for exactly the technique Gap 5/17 wants: turning free Wikipedia pageviews into a leading demand-attention signal with a public accuracy scoreboard and a graph/GNN structure that could be re-pointed at Airbnb/BKNG/EXPE/hotel-chain and destination-city Wikipedia pages instead of AI/pharma/EV entities.
candidates.size_hint: ~34 entities x daily pageviews since 2020, plus trained GNN checkpoints
candidates.last_activity: actively updated (daily CI as of query date)

candidates.name: influenza-wikipedia-dataset
candidates.what_it_holds: Committed dataset (4 stars) pairing influenza incidence surveillance data with Wikipedia pagecounts/pageviews for disease-related articles, built for infodemiology/nowcasting research.
candidates.why_useful: Off-theme (health, not travel) but a concrete precedent/template repo for 'Wikipedia pageviews of a topic committed alongside a real-world outcome series for nowcasting' - the exact data-shape a tourism-demand version of this project would need to produce; worth knowing as a methods reference rather than a direct data source.

candidates.name: global-nomad-atlas
candidates.what_it_holds: Open, community-maintained dataset (MIT, data snapshot 2026-08) scoring 80 digital-nomad cities across 40 countries (5 regions) on 12 dimensions (cost of living USD/month, internet quality, walkability, community strength, air quality, nightlife, safety, female-friendliness, LGBTQ+ acceptance, racial tolerance, English-friendliness) plus 60 coworking/coliving communities and a supplementary 16-city mainland-China dataset. Delivered as .xlsx and .csv files, PR-updatable.
candidates.why_useful: Directly touches Gap 16 (remote-work/long-stay demand, digital-nomad datasets) as a small but concrete, structured, city-level dataset that could proxy for long-stay/nomad demand geography relevant to Airbnb's long-term-stay segment, though it is a point-in-time snapshot (not a time series) and very new/low-traction (1 star).
candidates.geography: 80 cities, 40 countries (Asia 21, Europe 18, LatAm 15, Africa 7, Middle East 3) + 16 China cities
candidates.size_hint: 80 rows x 12 dimensions (+60-row community table, +16-row China supplement); xlsx/csv

notes: WebSearch was unavailable for this entire scout: the session had already exhausted its 200-query budget before my first call (shared session-wide, not a per-theme limit), so all discovery was done via WebFetch against GitHub topic pages (which worked) and github.com/search?q=... (which returned HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, Retry-After 3600, for every query attempted - likely a shared/prior-agent rate limit on the search endpoint specifically, since /topics/ pages fetched fine). This meant no true full-text GitHub code/repo search was possible; coverage leans on topic-page browsing and direct-URL guesses of well-known Wikipedia-pageviews tooling from general knowledge, then verification by WebFetch. A dedicated GitHub-search-capable pass (either `gh search` from a different modality, or WebSearch once the session budget resets) would likely surface tourism-specific academic replication packages (e.g. papers using Wikipedia pageviews to forecast international tourism demand for specific destinations) that pure topic-browsing could not find - github.com/topics/tourism-demand, travel-demand, tourism, web-traffic-prediction all came up empty or irrelevant for anything Wikipedia-specific. Recommend a follow-up scout on this exact theme once web search capacity is available, focused on: (1) academic replication code for papers titled around 'Wikipedia data-in-difference/gravity models of tourism demand' (Fronzetti Colladon, Rita, Bangwayo-Skeete-style authors), (2) Zenodo/OSF-hosted destination-pageview panels, (3) any GitHub mirror of the Kaggle Wikipedia Web Traffic dataset that includes the actual train_2.csv (some mirrors do commit it despite competition rules, which would remove the Kaggle-account friction). Zenodo's search UI did not return machine-readable results via WebFetch (JS-rendered), so that lead is unresolved, not negative.
